In their efforts to oppose commonsense reforms to strengthen Medicaid and ensure its sustainability for the most vulnerable and future Americans, Democrats are once again resorting to fear mongering—not facts.

Below is a breakdown of common Democratic myths and the real facts about the Big Beautiful Bill (BBB) Medicaid provisions:

⸻

DEMOCRAT FEAR MONGERING:

Millions will lose access to Medicaid under cruel new work requirements.

FACT:
The BBB’s Medicaid community engagement provisions apply only to able-bodied adults without dependents—not to seniors, people with disabilities, pregnant women, or caregivers.
Beginning January 1, 2026, these adults can meet the requirement by working, volunteering, attending school, or participating in job training for at least 80 hours a month.

This is not punitive—it’s empowering. It recognizes that Medicaid should support not just health but upward mobility and personal responsibility.

⸻

DEMOCRAT FEAR MONGERING:

Medicaid recipients will be kicked off the program due to paperwork errors and red tape.

FACT:
The BBB combats fraud, waste, and abuse, not eligible recipients.
For example, it ends the “good faith” waiver by 2030, ensuring states can no longer dodge accountability for improper payments to ineligible individuals or providers.

It uses the SSA Death Master File to prevent payments to deceased individuals and creates a federal system to prevent dual-state enrollment.

Verifying eligibility is not “red tape”—it’s responsible governance.

⸻

DEMOCRAT FEAR MONGERING:

The bill targets immigrants and punishes those in need.

FACT:
Federal law has long required that Medicaid recipients be citizens or legal residents.

The BBB strengthens enforcement by ending federal funding during the 90-day verification period for those without verified status.

No funding will go to those who are ineligible under federal law—this includes approximately 1.4 million illegal immigrants and 1.2 million other ineligible individuals who are currently on the rolls. 

⸻

DEMOCRAT FEAR MONGERING:

States will be penalized for trying to provide compassionate care.

FACT:
Beginning in 2028, states that deliberately fund health care for undocumented immigrants through Medicaid-like programs will face a 10% reduction in federal Medicaid matching funds.

This ensures that Medicaid remains focused on U.S. citizens and legal residents—the populations it was designed to serve.

⸻

DEMOCRAT FEAR MONGERING:

These changes are meant to slash Medicaid and gut funding.

FACT:
The BBB doesn’t slash Medicaid—it strengthens it.

By removing ineligible individuals and focusing resources on those truly in need, the reforms ensure long-term sustainability of the program.

Medicaid spending is projected to grow under the BBB, not shrink, because the focus is on integrity and efficiency—not cuts.

⸻

Bottom Line:
The BBB reforms don’t weaken Medicaid—they preserve it for those who need it most: vulnerable seniors, low-income children, people with disabilities, and legal working families.

It is important to note that a police state can emerge in authoritarian, totalitarian, or illiberal regimes, regardless of whether they are single-party or multi-party systems. A nonsensical federal classification is making it harder for Americans with diabetes to get vital treatment. 

Today I introduced the ISLET Act to change it and save lives. 

Here’s the situation:

For people living with Type 1 Diabetes, the immune system mistakenly attacks islet cells in the pancreas, which are responsible for producing insulin. 

Islets can be transplanted from deceased donors, allowing recipients to produce insulin naturally, reducing reliance on injections. Clinical trials have shown great improvement for patients with islet transplants. 

But the Food and Drug Administration currently classifies islets as drugs, subjecting them to a host of regulations that do not apply to organ transplants, slowing down life-saving procedures and limiting the practice in the United States, while it has become a standard of care in other countries. 

The Increase Support for Life-saving Endocrine Transplantation (ISLET) Act will correctly recategorize islets as organs, allowing widespread adoption of their medical use, and helping many Americans living with Type 1 Diabetes.

Many of you have reached out to my office with concerns about Glenn Medical Center, and I want to take a moment to share an update on where things stand.

As you may know, Willows' own Glenn Medical Center (GMC) is facing closure after twenty-four years of having “Critical Access Hospital” or CAH status, which allows GMC to receive a higher reimbursement rate and fewer regulatory burdens compared to other Medicare hospitals. CAH status is Glenn Medical’s lifeline for emergency healthcare in Glenn County. As the only emergency room in the county, without this status, the hospital will be forced to close its doors.

The revocation of this status is due to GMC no longer meeting the revised distance requirements as required by statute. Federal law requires a Critical Access Hospital to be over 35 miles from the next closest hospital, which in this case is Colusa Medical Center. Using I-5 and Highway 20, Glenn Medical Center is 35.7 miles away from Colusa Medical Center. However, the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) opted to change the calculation by using the rural cut-through of Maxwell Road, which now decreases the distance calculation to 32.5 miles, thereby putting Glenn Medical out of compliance. I am deeply frustrated about this decision, as the hospital has maintained its CAH status since 2001, and no new roads have been built, nor have the hospitals picked up and moved three miles closer during this time frame.

In 2001, Glenn Medical Center was on the brink of closure, but was saved when CMS designated it a Critical Access Hospital. CMS did not provide me with the routes used to calculate the distance requirement when GMC was first approved – CMS could not find the documentation. Then, in 2013, the Obama Administration released an Office of Inspector General report that concluded the majority of CAH-designated hospitals do not actually meet the statutory distance requirement. This resulted in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services reviewing the status of CAH-designated hospitals, including distance requirements, for compliance purposes.

Toward the end of the Obama Administration and the start of the first Trump Administration in about 2016, CMS began the process of recertifying CAH-designated hospitals every three to five years to ensure they still met the mileage requirement, and that no new roads or hospitals were built nearby. In 2017, CMS recertified Glenn Medical Center as a CAH, as this was during the nearly two-year span that Colusa Medical Center was closed. With Colusa Medical closed, GMC met the distance requirement at that time because no other hospitals were within 35 miles. During the pandemic years, CMS did not take action on recertifying CAH facilities as the main priority was keeping hospitals open.

This brings us to the end of the Biden Administration in December 2024, when Glenn Medical received a notice that it could potentially lose its CAH status. After receiving reassurance from CMS officials, the hospital believed it was in the clear, as it had maintained its status for over two decades. Despite these assurances, GMC’s CAH status was officially revoked in April of 2025, and its requests for mileage calculation reconsideration were denied in late August.

Since April, my team and I, along with GMC representatives, have actively engaged with CMS, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the White House to find a solution that would allow Glenn Medical to stay open. HHS officials initially indicated to me that CMS would likely restore GMC’s CAH status, but then abruptly changed course, saying it was constrained by the law, and a legislative fix was needed.

Throughout my conversations with CMS and Administrator Oz, my biggest argument was for government accountability and fairness. On a call with Dr. Oz, CMS admitted that it should have never given Glenn Medical Center its CAH status in the first place. According to Dr. Oz, it was a mistake made by CMS 24 years ago, and there was nothing he could do to restore GMC’s CAH status. Because of that “mistake,” now the residents of Glenn County are paying the price. This is not how government is supposed to operate – it’s unfair and just plain wrong. I refuse to believe CMS’s hands are tied, and I will do everything in my power to fix this situation for Glenn County.

I have not given up on Glenn Medical Center and will continue to work to obtain a permanent fix on its CAH status, pursuing every option available. I am working directly with House Leadership and the White House to grant additional time before the CAH status is phased out, and have sought to include a fix in a recent bill, but it was not successful. It did put the issue on record. Simultaneously, I am asking for the Administration to set aside dollars from the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which was passed in H.R. 1, and is specifically geared to assist in keeping rural hospitals afloat. I am also working with Congressional leadership and relevant House committees to craft legislation to help restore Glenn Medical’s CAH status.

Unfortunately, Glenn Medical Center has announced the closure of its emergency room on September 30th as it no longer has enough staff to remain viable. California’s strict staffing ratio laws also placed additional burdens on Glenn Medical’s ability to keep the doors open. While Glenn Medical does not officially lose CAH reimbursement rates until April of 2026, the discouragement of staff has led to an exodus that has unfortunately outpaced the legislative process. I remain hopeful that an administrative extension of their status and a permanent legislative fix can be done this Congressional session, and we may be able to revive Glenn Medical Center.

I haven’t given up on Glenn Medical Center. My priority in Washington is making sure the people of Northern California are represented, and I will continue to battle for a solution.

Medicaid (called Medi-Cal here in California) is supposed to be a safety net for children, people with disabilities, and low-income families. The new budget reconciliation law strengthens that system by making sure it’s focused on those who truly rely on it.

Here’s what’s changing. Able-bodied adults without young kids who choose not to work will now be expected to work, volunteer, or pursue education at least 80 hours a month to keep getting benefits. It’s a commonsense, bipartisan idea that promotes stability and leads to better health outcomes.

At the same time, the law tightens eligibility checks and steps up verification of citizenship and immigration status to help crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse. Over the last decade, improper Medicaid payments have totaled more than half a trillion dollars nationwide, with $56 billion just last year. That’s unacceptable.

For states like California that have pushed Medicaid far beyond its original scope, the law gradually scales back certain federal matching rates, meaning states will pick up a fairer share of the costs. It also closes loopholes that let states draw down extra federal money without actually improving care.

As for concerns about rural healthcare, the law provides $10 billion a year for five years, totaling $50 billion, to help keep small rural hospitals and clinics open. How that money gets distributed in California will come down to the Governor and state officials. The budget reconciliation package updates the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by returning to mandatory work requirements and tighter accountability designed to strengthen the program and ensure it serves those who need it most.

Waivers from these rules will be limited to areas with high unemployment, making sure states like California can't exempt the entire state from the work requirement.

Benefit increases going forward will be capped to track inflation, preventing unchecked growth without Congressional approval.

For the first time, states will be responsible for a portion of actual SNAP food benefit costs, not just administrative expenses, encouraging stronger financial stewardship at the state level. The formula for state matching funds will be updated to reflect recent payment error rates, promoting better oversight and reducing waste. When states don't have skin in the game to ensure payment accuracy, the high error rates hurt SNAP recipients the most.

These changes are about making SNAP more accountable, sustainable, and focused on helping Americans get back to work.
